analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal commission to regulate large online platforms' competition, privacy, and algorithms.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2022 with zero cosponsors, sat in three House committees and died when the Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new Federal Digital Platform Commission — a five-member regulator, similar in design to the FCC or FTC — to write rules for large online platforms. It would set standards for how platforms' algorithms work, require public risk assessments and third-party audits, mandate data portability and interoperability so users can leave a platform with their data, require government review before big platforms are sold or merged, and let individuals and state attorneys general sue platforms over violations. It would single out 'systemically important' platforms — the very largest ones — for the strictest rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use large social media, search, and shopping platforms. The bill would give users protections against deceptive or unfair platform practices, more transparency about how content is ranked and moderated, accessibility standards for people with disabilities, and a right to complain to the commission or sue in court. Small businesses that depend on big platforms to reach customers would benefit from data portability, interoperability, and merger review that could slow acquisitions of competitors.

how_it_helps.text: The commission would be required to write rules for the largest platforms covering data portability, interoperability, algorithmic fairness and transparency, content moderation transparency, and public risk assessments of harmful content, with third-party audits [S3].
The bill creates a private right of action: any person claiming harm from a digital platform could sue in federal court, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents [S3].

Large platforms could not be sold or merged without the commission finding the transfer serves the public interest, and platforms could be fined up to 1% of global daily revenue for failing to file required reports [S3].

The bill directs the commission to protect competition, prevent harmful concentration of private power over digital infrastructure, and shield consumers from deceptive, unfair, or abusive platform practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest digital platform companies, which would bear the cost of compliance, audits, mandatory disclosures, merger applications, and potential fines and private lawsuits. Taxpayers would fund the new agency, with authorized appropriations rising from $100 million in fiscal 2023 to $500 million per year by 2027 [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would create a powerful new agency with broad rulemaking authority over services that carry political speech, and critics of platform regulation argue this risks government entanglement with online expression; the bill itself repeatedly invokes First Amendment limits as a guardrail [S3].

Compliance costs, mandatory disclosures, and the need to win commission approval before any sale would fall on the largest platforms, and opponents argue those costs could slow innovation or be passed to users and advertisers.

A five-member commission appointed by the President would hold sweeping discretion over which platforms are 'systemically important' and what rules they must follow, a design some would view as concentrating too much power in too few hands; the bill does provide for a five-year independent review of whether the commission should continue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give users and small businesses real tools — transparency, portability, court access — against a handful of companies with enormous power over commerce and public debate, at the price of a new $500-million-a-year agency and compliance burdens on the platforms. The main honest concerns are the breadth of the agency's discretion over speech-adjacent services and the risk of heavy-handed rules, but the bill builds in exemptions for small platforms and news organizations, an industry Code Council with a seat at the table, and a scheduled five-year sunset review. The larger design question went untested, because the bill never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, no committee ever took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the Digital Platform Commission Act of 2022 in the House on May 19, 2022 [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means and Small Business Committees [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, and the record shows no further action after the referrals; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large digital platforms that the bill would have regulated, along with the members of Congress who never had to vote on it. Users, small businesses, and state enforcers gained nothing from the bill's death, but they also lost nothing beyond the protections it would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large digital platforms dodged new regulation

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill establishing a Federal Digital Platform Commission on May 19, 2022

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (primary committee of referral)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing; the committee record shows no action after the bill's referral, and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended

against.name: House Small Business and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; it died with the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no cosponsor from either party signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never measured.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms (social media, search, e-commerce, app ecosystems)
industries.note: The bill would subject the largest platforms to algorithmic transparency rules, mandatory audits, merger approval, data portability and interoperability standards, daily fines up to 1% of global revenue for missing reports, and private lawsuits. Its death leaves their largely self-regulated status quo intact [S3].

The bill exempts small platform businesses from regulation while requiring interoperability and data portability from the giants and reviewing their acquisitions — changes that would make it easier for small firms to compete and resist buyouts [S3].

News publishers are excluded from the definition of a regulated digital platform, and the bill's findings cite platform dominance as a driver of the collapse of local journalism; regulation of the platforms would have been the indirect benefit [S3].
